t: Old English grew from the dialects of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled in Britain in the 5th century, and it replaced the Common Brittonic and Latin of Roman Britain over most of what became England.

It was a heavily inflected language, with five cases, three genders and a freer word order than Modern English; perhaps around 85% of its words are no longer in use, but those that survived are the basic elements of English vocabulary.

Under Alfred the Great, and later the Winchester standard of Bishop Æthelwold, it became a written language of government and literature, until the Norman Conquest of 1066 made Anglo-Norman French the language of the upper classes.
dyk: With few and relatively unimportant exceptions, all surviving Old English poetry is preserved in just four manuscripts; the earliest English poet known by name, Cædmon, was a lay brother at the monastery of Whitby.
ev: Anglo-Saxon settlers bring to Britain the dialects that become Old English
Cædmon composes his hymn, the oldest surviving work of Old English literature
The Franks Casket is carved with the oldest coherent runic texts in Old English
Scandinavian rule and settlement begin, bringing strong Old Norse influence to the speech of eastern and northern England
Alfred the Great unites the kingdoms outside the Danelaw, and West Saxon becomes the standard language of government and literature
A new literary standard, Late West Saxon, arises at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold
Cnut addresses a proclamation in Old English to Earl Thorkell the Tall and the English people
The Norman Conquest: Anglo-Norman replaces English as the language of the upper classes

f.family: West Germanic, from the Anglo-Frisian or Ingvaeonic (North Sea Germanic) dialects of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes; its closest relatives are Old Frisian and Old Saxon
f.script: runes of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc (5th–7th centuries); the Latin alphabet, introduced in the 7th century by Irish missionaries and supplanting the runes from around the 8th, in half-uncial and then Insular script, with the added letters æ, ð, þ and ƿ
f.earliest: a small corpus of runic inscriptions of the 5th to 7th centuries; Cædmon’s Hymn, composed between 658 and 680 and written down in the early 8th century; the runic texts of the Franks Casket, early 8th century
f.status: extinct; after the Norman Conquest of 1066 it developed into Middle English and so into Modern English, while its Northumbrian dialect became the source of Scots
